title: Workflows Break Across Roles
summary: This page defines a workflow failure that appears at role boundaries in multi-role software. It distinguishes role-boundary failure from intra-role navigation overhead and from broader attention-overhead failures, then describes the three main forms: lost handoff context, single-interface mismatch, and incompatible mental models across a handoff.
keyFacts: The failure occurs where one role's output becomes another role's input, not simply where one user has too many screens or steps.
The three described forms are handoffs that lose context, single-interface incompatibility across role groups, and incompatible mental models across a handoff.
In high-consequence and regulated contexts, broken role-boundary workflows can weaken verification, audit trails, approvals, and governance processes.
The Akrivia Health example concerns a researcher-to-governance-reviewer handoff where cohort construction had to remain independently readable for verification.
The Animana example distinguishes reception staff and clinical staff as different role groups with different cognitive modes and role-specific workarounds.

The Pixelart Fugo example concerns a mismatch between multi-location scheduling work and a single-location schedule architecture; NPS moved from 57% to 89% after redesign, client-measured before and after.

The Triopsis example involved schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians; field-measured product analytics reported 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning.

The UNICEF example concerned incompatible interpretations of reporting requirements across seven role types and two organisational tiers; client-measured outcomes included a 45% reduction in compliance issues and a 42% reduction in headquarters report-preparation time.
Assemblio described a planning tool used by engineers and a shop-floor application used by assembly workers; Assemblio's product accounts are client-stated, not field-observed by Creative Navy.

bodySections.heading: Role-boundary workflow failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Workflows break across roles when multi-role software is specified role by role but not across the boundary between roles. The analyst view may be coherent for analysts, the reviewer interface may be coherent for reviewers, and the scheduler screen may be coherent for schedulers, while the workflow that connects those roles is left unspecified.

A role-boundary workflow failure appears where one role's completed work becomes another role's starting point. If the system does not carry the receiving role's required context, task state, information, reasoning, or standard of correctness, the receiving role depends on clarification or correction outside the system.

bodySections.heading: Why role-boundary workflow failure is not ordinary navigation overhead
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Workflows that break across roles should be distinguished from tasks that span too many screens or steps. Tasks that span too many screens or steps create navigation overhead inside one role's work. Workflows that break across roles fail at the point where one role's completed task becomes another role's starting point.

This failure also overlaps with, but is narrower than, excessive attention requirements in routine use. A single interface serving multiple roles with incompatible cognitive requirements can create attention overhead. The role-boundary workflow failure is the specific workflow consequence: the system does not support the crossing between role groups, or it imposes one role's logic on another role's work.

In high-consequence and regulated contexts, role-boundary workflow failure can become a structural oversight problem. Governance review, audit trails, compliance checks, approval cycles, and execution quality often depend on a receiving role being able to inspect or continue work produced by another role.

bodySections.heading: Three forms of role-boundary workflow failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Role-boundary workflow failure has three documented forms in the available material: handoffs that lose context, single-interface incompatibility across role groups, and incompatible mental models across a handoff.

Handoffs lose context when the reasoning that shaped a task on one side of a role boundary does not survive the crossing in interpretable form. The producing role may understand why a query, schedule, submission, or assignment was assembled in a particular way. The receiving role sees the result but not the reasoning that would make independent verification possible.

Single-interface incompatibility occurs when multiple roles with different cognitive requirements, task models, and error profiles are forced through one interface architecture. The failure is not confined to one handoff point. It appears wherever the shared interface reflects the wrong role's operating logic.

Incompatible mental models occur when information crosses the role boundary intact, but the roles on either side interpret the same requirement, field, or standard differently. The failure is not transmission. The failure is the absence of a shared definition of what the submitted work must satisfy.

bodySections.heading: Akrivia Health: researcher-to-governance-reviewer readability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Akrivia Health clinical research platform is an example of handoff context loss. Researchers assembled cohorts by specifying nested logical inclusion and exclusion criteria. Governance reviewers at NHS trusts, academic institutions, and pharmaceutical research organisations needed to verify that the completed cohort query matched an approved study protocol.

The design problem was not only cohort construction. The role-boundary problem was whether the researcher's construction logic remained readable to the governance reviewer at the handoff.

Creative Navy's design work on Akrivia treated the researcher's construction task and the governance reviewer's verification task separately. The resulting query builder allowed flexible cohort construction while maintaining the reasoning structure in independently readable form. Akrivia client-reported that governance reviewers could verify cohort construction without escalating to the research team; this outcome was client-reported and not independently measured.

bodySections.heading: Animana and Pixelart Fugo: incompatible interfaces for different role groups
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Animana engagement documented single-interface incompatibility across reception staff and clinical staff. Field research across 35 clinics in three countries established that reception staff worked in ambient multitasking under time pressure and needed breadth, speed, and access to frequent actions. Clinical staff, including vets and nurses, worked in focused sequential case attention and needed depth, completeness, and full case history.

The diagnostic signal in Animana was role-specific workaround behaviour. Checklists taped to monitors appeared near reception terminals rather than clinical workstations. Printed reference sheets near terminals were for reception-specific workflows rather than clinical ones. The workarounds indicated role-specific interface failure rather than a general usability problem.

Pixelart Fugo showed the same type of incompatibility in scheduling architecture. Content producers, such as media agencies, needed to assign content across 20 or 40 locations simultaneously. The existing platform had been built around a single-location, location-specific schedule model. The redesign replaced a wizard organised around the internal playlist object model with an overview structure organised around what content plays, where it plays, and when it plays. NPS moved from 57% to 89% after the redesign, client-measured before and after.

bodySections.heading: UNICEF: incompatible interpretations of reporting requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The UNICEF planning, approval, and reporting tool is an example of incompatible mental models across a handoff. The tool was operated by seven role types across two organisational tiers, plus a conditional external user class. Local roles included a Country Programme Manager, Project Directors or Project Officers, and where present Finance Officers. Central roles included a Planning & Reporting Manager and a Finance Manager. Submissions had to satisfy both central functions to be accepted.

Many compliance failures did not come from users being unable to operate the interface. They emerged because work that was technically correct from a project perspective could be incomplete from a finance perspective; a financial revision could invalidate information entered elsewhere; approvals could be assumed without formal recording; and different contributors could hold different interpretations of a reporting requirement's purpose.

Creative Navy's Sandbox Experiments phase produced 26 prototypes reviewed by 56 stakeholders across both tiers. The prototypes were used to establish a shared understanding of what each requirement was for and which requirements were necessary. Once the shared standards were agreed, the redesigned system embedded them through workflows, validation rules, information architecture, and interaction design. Client-measured outcomes nine months after rollout included a 45% reduction in compliance issues and a 42% reduction in headquarters report-preparation time.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis: three-role workforce management failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Triopsis served schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians in one workforce management platform. The scheduling workflow connected the three roles: schedulers assigned jobs, operations managers monitored the resulting schedule and managed exceptions, and field technicians executed assigned work.

The role-boundary problem was that the information that mattered at each crossing was different from what the current view showed. Schedulers needed to see job-sequence conflicts before they became execution failures. Operations managers needed exception-first monitoring rather than equal attention to routine and exceptional items. Field technicians needed immediate job instructions rather than a planning-oriented view.

Three in-situ observation sessions established the breakdown points between roles. The redesign introduced predictive conflict indicators for schedulers, exception-first organisation for operations managers, and clear job-level instructions for field technicians. Field-measured product analytics from real users in the live product recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio: client-stated role-specific product separation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio described two products serving two user populations: Assemblio Composer, the planning tool used by engineers, and Assemblio Smart Viewer, the shop-floor application used by assembly workers. Assemblio's accounts of its own product are client-stated rather than observed by Creative Navy.

The Smart Viewer had been built from the Composer's components and looked almost identical to it, although the requirements for engineers and assembly workers differed. Assemblio described a complete CAD hierarchy being shown at all times in the Smart Viewer, reflecting the engineer's structure, while the worker needed the parts used in the current step.

Assemblio's worked example was a step containing two visually similar types of screw where the names in the list did not tell the worker which was which. Assemblio also described that the worker had no way to send feedback back to the planner when a step did not work in practice. The workflow broke in both directions: the engineer's structure flowed down in a form not shaped for the worker's task, and the worker's practical feedback did not flow back up.

Separating the Smart Viewer from the Composer as two products for two populations was Assemblio's own diagnosis. Creative Navy's contribution concerned what the second product should become, not the initial recognition that two populations needed different products.

bodySections.heading: How Critical Systems Design addresses role-boundary workflow failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For role-boundary workflow failures, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method models each role's cognitive requirements separately before designing for interaction between roles. Separate role modelling is used to identify which differences are genuine operational requirements and which differences indicate a design problem.

Sandbox Experiments can use multiple role groups against each other to reveal where an interface needs to hold different requirements simultaneously. In Akrivia, separate work with NHS analysts, academic researchers, and pharmaceutical research staff showed that governance requirements differed institutionally and needed to be handled explicitly. In Animana, separate work with reception staff and clinical staff, including attention to role-specific workarounds, established that the failure was role-specific. In UNICEF, research across both organisational tiers showed that the client had mis-diagnosed a mental-model mismatch as local-office reluctance.

Concept Convergence addresses the architecture of the handoff. In Akrivia, the query builder held researcher flexibility and governance readability in the same query architecture. In Pixelart Fugo, the overview structure held media-agency multi-location scheduling and organisation-level screen management in the same operational model: what content plays, where it plays, and when it plays.

For the mental-model form, the design work begins upstream of interface detail. Where no shared standard exists, designing the handoff first requires establishing the standard that the handoff is supposed to carry. The UNICEF prototypes served this function before the agreed standards were embedded in workflows, validation rules, information architecture, and interaction design.

bodySections.heading: Design responses depend on the specific role boundary
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Role-boundary workflow failure should not be read as a claim that every multi-role interface must become separate products or separate screens. The documented cases show that the right design response depends on the specific boundary.

Some role boundaries require reasoning to be carried across the handoff. Some require incompatible role views to be separated. Some require an internal object model to be replaced with an operational model. Some require a shared standard to be established before interface design can produce a reliable handoff.

strongClaims: Workflows break across roles when a system fails to carry context, information, task state, or shared standards from one role's work into another role's work.
The failure has three documented forms: handoffs that lose context, single-interface incompatibility across role groups, and incompatible mental models across a handoff.
In Pixelart Fugo, NPS moved from 57% to 89% after redesign, client-measured before and after.
In Triopsis, product analytics from real users in the live system recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning.
In UNICEF, client-measured outcomes nine months after rollout included a 45% reduction in compliance issues and a 42% reduction in headquarters report-preparation time.
weakerClaims: In the Akrivia Health example, the query builder allowed researcher flexibility while keeping the query logic readable for governance reviewers; Akrivia client-reported that reviewers could verify cohort construction without escalating to the research team.
Assemblio's product and operating-context details are client-stated rather than field-observed by Creative Navy.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses role-boundary failures by modelling role requirements separately and designing the interaction between roles rather than only the screens used by each role.
limitations: The page describes a failure pattern and grounded examples; it does not establish that every multi-role system has this failure.
Akrivia's governance-reviewer outcome is client-reported and not independently measured.
Pixelart Fugo's NPS outcome is client-measured before and after; the source does not provide independent measurement details.
UNICEF's compliance and report-preparation outcomes are client-measured; the page preserves the stated measurement basis and timeframe.

Assemblio evidence is limited to client-stated product and operating-context descriptions. Creative Navy did not conduct shop-floor observation, field research, safety analysis, or usability measurement in that engagement.
No time-saving, error-rate, training, or adoption figure is claimed for Assemblio.
